what: Browser auth is about where the login proof lives and who can steal it. The safest common design is a Backend For Frontend (BFF): the server does the OAuth login with PKCE, keeps the tokens, and gives the browser only an HttpOnly session cookie, protected against CSRF.
like: Like a school front office: the student never carries the master key; the office holds it and hands out a hall pass (cookie) that only works on school grounds.
why: Tokens in JavaScript-readable storage are stolen by any XSS bug
Cookies are sent automatically, so they need CSRF defences
Refresh tokens are long-lived and powerful, so they should stay server-side where possible

nodes.t: Resource APIs|get access token from BFF

steps.d: The app sends the user to the authorization server with a random code challenge and a state value. PKCE ties the returned code to the party that started the flow, and state/nonce blocks CSRF on the redirect.
The BFF is a confidential client: it swaps the code for tokens using its own credentials plus the PKCE verifier, so tokens never touch the browser.
The BFF sets a cookie with HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite, ideally with the __Host- prefix (no Domain, Path=/). JavaScript cannot read it.
The SPA calls /api on the same site; the BFF looks up the session, attaches the access token and forwards to the resource server, only to an allow-list of hosts and paths.
Because the cookie rides along automatically, require a custom header such as X-CSRF-Token on state-changing calls, check Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site, and keep SameSite on.

steps.t: Refresh and log out on the server
steps.d: Refresh tokens are rotated or sender-constrained and live only in the BFF store. Logout deletes the server session and the cookie so tokens are dead everywhere.

numbers.l: architectures in the IETF browser-based apps draft, safest first: BFF, token-mediating backend, browser-only client
default SameSite treatment when a cookie sets no SameSite attribute
requirements of the __Host- cookie prefix, plus Secure over HTTPS

choices.t: BFF cookie or tokens in the browser
choices.d: BFF keeps tokens off the page and the draft recommends it for sensitive and personal-data apps. Tokens in the browser are simpler to host but exposed to XSS and token theft.

choices.t: Cookie or localStorage for a session
choices.d: HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by injected script but needs CSRF protection; localStorage is not sent automatically but any script on the origin can read it, so one XSS leaks it.
An opaque session id is easy to revoke on the server. A self-contained JWT scales without lookups but is hard to revoke; keep lifetimes short and do not put secrets inside it.
Same site lets SameSite=Strict cookies work simply. A cross-origin API needs credentials: 'include', exact-origin CORS with Allow-Credentials, and SameSite=None; Secure with weaker CSRF protection.

instead.why: The storage and cookie-attribute details underneath this block
XSS is the main way browser tokens get stolen, so prevent it first

breaks.d: Access or refresh token in localStorage is read by an injected script.
breaks.see: Same token used from another IP or device
breaks.fix: Move tokens behind a BFF with HttpOnly cookie; short access tokens, rotate refresh tokens

breaks.d: A malicious site makes the browser send a state-changing request with the cookie.
breaks.see: Unexpected POSTs with a foreign Origin
breaks.fix: SameSite, custom header requirement, Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site checks, and no state change on GET

breaks.d: Many tabs refresh at once; rotation invalidates the winner's token.
breaks.fix: Do refresh on the server in one place, single-flight the call, and queue requests that arrive during it

say: I would use a BFF: the server runs the Authorization Code flow with PKCE as a confidential client and the browser holds only an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite session cookie.
The BFF attaches the access token when it proxies API calls and keeps refresh tokens server-side with rotation, so an XSS bug cannot exfiltrate long-lived credentials.
Because it is cookie based, we add CSRF defences: a required custom header, Origin or Fetch Metadata checks, and SameSite, on top of strong XSS prevention.

followups.q: Why PKCE if the BFF is confidential?
followups.a: A confidential client authenticates with its own credentials, but PKCE is still good practice and is required for public clients. If the app is a pure SPA with no backend, PKCE is mandatory.

followups.q: Is a JWT in localStorage ever fine?
followups.a: It is a trade-off for low-risk apps. Any XSS can read it, so for sensitive data prefer the BFF cookie; if you must hold a token in the browser, keep it in memory, short lived, with a strict CSP.
SameSite cookies, a synchronizer or signed double-submit token, custom headers that force a CORS preflight, and Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site checks. XSS defeats all of them, so prevent XSS too.

today: The IETF guidance OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications is now RFC 10017 (BCP 212, August 2026). It ranks BFF first, token-mediating backend second and a browser-only client last, requires PKCE for public clients and rotation or sender-constraining of refresh tokens.

check.q: What is the draft's most secure pattern for a browser app?
check.a: Backend For Frontend with tokens kept server-side and a cookie session
d: Refresh token in a JavaScript variable shared across tabs
Embedding the client secret in the bundle
check.why: The BFF is a confidential client and the browser never sees tokens.

check.q: Which cookie attributes protect a session cookie from script access and plain HTTP?
check.why: HttpOnly hides it from document.cookie and Secure restricts it to HTTPS.

check.q: Why add a custom header requirement on API calls?
check.a: Cross-site pages cannot send it without a CORS preflight that you control
check.why: Browsers preflight custom headers cross-origin, so only allowed origins can set it.
